analysis.one_liner: Requires big outside election spenders to reveal their top funders and bans campaign spending by federal contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 49 Senate cosponsors — every Democrat and independent who backed it — but died in the Senate Rules Committee without a hearing or vote; a House companion passed but Senate Republicans blocked it from reaching the floor.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision allowed corporations and unions to spend unlimited money on elections, this bill would have forced the biggest funders of campaign ads to be named — on screen, in reports, and to shareholders. It would have barred companies holding federal contracts worth $50,000 or more from making campaign expenditures, applied the ban on foreign money to foreign-controlled U.S. corporations, treated coordinated spending as a contribution, and required registered lobbyists to report their campaign spending. It never got out of committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would see the names of the top five funders behind television ads and hear disclosure statements on radio ads; shareholders and members of corporations and unions, who would learn how their organizations' money is spent politically; and candidates, who would buy advertising airtime at the lowest unit rate rather than premium prices.

how_it_helps.text: Requires any organization running election ads to disclose its top funders, including a 'Top 5 Funders' list displayed on television ads for at least six seconds, so viewers know who is paying [S2] [S3].

Bars companies with federal contracts of $50,000 or more, and recipients of TARP bailout assistance, from making independent expenditures or electioneering communications, to keep public contracting separate from campaign influence [S2] [S3].
Extends the existing ban on foreign money in elections to U.S. corporations controlled by foreign nationals, with a CEO certification requirement [S2] [S3].

Requires anyone spending more than $10,000 on independent expenditures to report it within 24 hours, and expands the window during which ads count as electioneering communications from 60 to 90 days before a primary [S2] [S3].

Requires registered lobbyists to report their own independent expenditures and electioneering communications of $1,000 or more, so the public can connect campaign spending to lobbying activity [S2] [S3].

Requires covered organizations to tell shareholders, members, and donors how their money was used for campaign activity, and extends lowest-unit-charge ad rates so candidates pay less for airtime [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, labor unions, and tax-exempt groups that spend money on federal elections would bear new reporting, certification, and on-air disclosure costs; government contractors and foreign-controlled corporations would lose the ability to spend treasury money on elections; and broadcasters would earn less from political ads under the lowest-unit-rate rules.

drawbacks.text: The compliance load is heavy: organizations spending $10,000 or more must report within 24 hours, CEOs must certify under penalty of perjury how treasury funds are used, and tracking every donor who must be named in an ad is costly, especially for small nonprofits and membership groups [S3].

The redefinition of an independent expenditure to include anything that is the 'functional equivalent of express advocacy' sweeps in communications that do not explicitly say 'vote for' or 'vote against,' a standard critics said was vague enough to chill speech by groups that merely discuss a candidate's record [S3].

Good-faith objections held that mandatory donor disclosure could expose rank-and-file members and donors of unpopular causes to harassment, even though disclosure aims to inform voters — a tension the bill acknowledges by allowing donors to opt out in writing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is straightforward: voters would know who is behind the ads trying to sway their votes, and the bill is carefully engineered to trace money transferred between groups. The costs fall on organizations that spend on politics, and the compliance burden is real but aimed at the very entities that just gained the right to spend unlimited treasury funds. The main design criticism is that the broad 'functional equivalent of express advocacy' standard and tight deadlines create compliance risk for small groups while big spenders can afford lawyers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended; a House companion bill did pass the House, but when Senate leaders brought that version up in the fall of 2010, it fell short of the 60 votes needed to move forward.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 30, 2010 by Sen. Schumer with 37 original cosponsors, four months after the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision opened the door to unlimited corporate and union treasury spending in elections [S1] [S3].
Forty-nine senators — 47 Democrats, one independent, and one independent Democrat — cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration the day it was introduced, and the record shows no further Senate action — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S5].

A companion bill passed the House in June 2010, and Senate Democratic leaders brought campaign-spending disclosure to the floor in September 2010, but the vote fell well short of the 60 needed to break a Republican filibuster (widely reported).
The Congress ended on January 3, 2011 with the bill still in committee [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Outside groups that gained the right to spend unlimited corporate, union, and nonprofit treasury money on elections after Citizens United are better off, because no disclosure regime was enacted; government contractors and foreign-controlled corporations also avoided new spending bans. Ordinary voters got no new information about who funds campaign ads.

sides.party_line_note: All 49 cosponsors were Democrats or independents and no Republican signed on; the House companion passed on a mostly party-line vote while Senate Republicans united to block it.

industries.industry: Corporations and trade groups spending on elections
industries.note: The bill ends their ability to spend unlimited treasury money anonymously in elections and to buy influence while holding federal contracts; the public gains the funders' names behind every ad.
These groups exist to move money into politics without naming donors; the bill forces them to list top funders in reports and on-screen in ads, directly threatening their fundraising model.

Unions are covered organizations under the bill and would face the same reporting, certification, and ad-disclosure burdens as corporations, though transparency rules apply to them equally and their members would see how dues-funded money is spent.
Extending lowest-unit-charge rates to more political buyers and parties cuts into the premium rates stations charge during election season; candidates and voters benefit from cheaper airtime.
Lobbyists would have to report their own campaign expenditures, exposing the link between lobbying clients and election spending.
